To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the probability that an unemployed worker will seek retraining declines with the age of the worker, with the worker being attached to contracting industries, and with the worker being content with the previous job.
The probability of seeking re-training declines with age after 27 years; with being in a non-contracting industry; and with contentment in unemployment.

(1) the probability of seeking training declines with age after 27; with being attached in non-contracting industries; with higher contentment in unemployment than in the last job; and, with union membership.

the authors have made a significant contribution to the literature on the determinants of retraining, and to the literature on labour market flows.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the paper is a useful contribution to a neglected area, and it is a good example of the way that econometrics may be applied to the study of labour market behaviour.

we have shown that the human capital model of training is consistent with the observed behaviour of unemployed workers, and that the model is a useful tool for analysing the behaviour of unemployed workers.
the unemployed do not seek retraining as much as the literature suggests.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the demand for retraining is not simply a function of the duration of unemployment, but is influenced by the characteristics of the unemployed and their last job.
the probability of retraining application is increased by the presence of a job offer and is decreased by the presence of an active job search.
the probability of applying for training is higher for younger workers, for workers in non-contracting industries and for workers with higher levels of education.
